claim: The Hydra nervous system consists of 500-2000 nerve cells, depending on animal size.
source: With a nervous system consisting of only 500–2000 nerve cells, depending on animal size (Bode et al., 1973), the freshwater cnidarian polyp Hydra is a particularly useful model organism for such investigations.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bode et al., 1973.

claim: There are only two types of nerve cells in Hydra based on morphology: ganglion cells and sensory cells.
source: Furthermore, there are only two types of nerve cells in Hydra based on morphology: ganglion cells and sensory cells, and there are no surrounding support cells, such as glial cells in bilaterians (David, 1973; Epp and Tardent, 1978; Westfall, 1973; Westfall and Epp, 1985).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to David, 1973; Epp and Tardent, 1978; Westfall, 1973; Westfall and Epp, 1985.

claim: There are no surrounding support cells, such as glial cells, in Hydra.
source: Furthermore, there are only two types of nerve cells in Hydra based on morphology: ganglion cells and sensory cells, and there are no surrounding support cells, such as glial cells in bilaterians (David, 1973; Epp and Tardent, 1978; Westfall, 1973; Westfall and Epp, 1985).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to David, 1973; Epp and Tardent, 1978; Westfall, 1973; Westfall and Epp, 1985.

claim: Ganglion cells in Hydra are bipolar or multipolar.
source: Ganglion cells are bipolar or multipolar, but there is no evidence for a distinction between axons and dendrites.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: There is no evidence for a distinction between axons and dendrites in Hydra ganglion cells.
source: Ganglion cells are bipolar or multipolar, but there is no evidence for a distinction between axons and dendrites.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: Sensory nerve cells in Hydra are polarized, with a short neurite and sensory cilium at one pole and a longer neurite at the opposite pole.
source: Sensory nerve cells, by comparison, are polarized, with a short neurite and sensory cilium at one pole and a longer neurite at the opposite pole.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: Sensory cells in the ectoderm extend a cilium to the surface of the epithelium to sense the external environment.
source: Sensory cells in the ectoderm extend a cilium to the surface of the epithelium to sense the external environment.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: Sensory cells in the endoderm extend a cilium into the gastric cavity.
source: Sensory cells in the endoderm extend a cilium into the gastric cavity.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: Recent scRNAseq results have refined morphological classes to include three sensory and five ganglion nerve cell populations based on distinct transcriptomes.
source: Recent scRNAseq results have refined these morphological classes to include three sensory and five ganglion nerve cell populations based on distinct transcriptomes (Cazet et al., 2023; Siebert et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cazet et al., 2023 and Siebert et al., 2019.

claim: All Hydra tissues, including the nerve net, are newly formed every 2-3 weeks in well-fed animals.
source: All Hydra tissues, including the nerve net, are newly formed every 2–3 weeks in well-fed animals (Campbell, 1967; David and Campbell, 1972; David and Gierer, 1974).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Campbell, 1967; David and Campbell, 1972; David and Gierer, 1974.

claim: Cell proliferation in Hydra occurs exclusively in the body column.
source: Since cell proliferation occurs exclusively in the body column, there is continuous displacement of cells from the body column toward the head and foot and loss of cells at the extremities.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: Tentacle tissue is completely renewed in 4-5 days by displacement of epithelial tissue from the body column into the tentacles.
source: Tentacle tissue is completely renewed in 4–5 days by displacement of epithelial tissue from the body column into the tentacles.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: PNab stains all nerve cells and nerve processes in fixed Hydra polyps.
source: In the present experiments, we take advantage of a newly developed pan-neuronal antibody (PNab), which stains all nerve cells and nerve processes in fixed Hydra polyps.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by experimental validation described in the Results section.

claim: Nerve cells in Hydra are organized as two separate nerve nets, one in the ectoderm and one in the endoderm.
source: Antibody staining and confocal microscopy show that nerve cells in Hydra are organized as two separate nerve nets, one in the ectoderm and one in the endoderm.
evidence: The claim is supported by antibody staining and confocal microscopy data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The two nerve nets in Hydra consist of discrete bundles of overlapping nerve cell processes.
source: Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and block face scanning electron microscopy (SEM) demonstrate that the two nerve nets consist of discrete bundles of overlapping nerve cell processes.
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM and block face SEM data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The nerve nets in the ectoderm and endoderm do not contact each other.
source: The nerve nets in the ectoderm and endoderm do not contact each other.
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: There is an unexpected absence of nerve cells in the endoderm of the tentacles.
source: Confocal imaging shows that there are two distinct nerve nets, one in the ectoderm and one in the endoderm, with the unexpected absence of nerve cells in the endoderm of the tentacles.
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Nerve cell-specific innexins indicate that gap junctions can provide circuit specificity.
source: Nerve cell-specific innexins indicate that gap junctions can provide this specificity.
evidence: The claim is supported by scRNAseq data and TEM images showing gap junctions.

claim: The occurrence of bundles of neurites supports a model for continuous growth and differentiation of the nerve net by lateral addition of new nerve cells to the existing net.
source: The occurrence of bundles of neurites supports a model for continuous growth and differentiation of the nerve net by lateral addition of new nerve cells to the existing net.
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from the structural observations and confirmed by tracking experiments.

claim: The model for nerve net growth by lateral addition was confirmed by tracking newly differentiated nerve cells.
source: This model was confirmed by tracking newly differentiated nerve cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from grafting experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: All NeonGreen-expressing nerve cells (684/684) in the alpha-tubulin transgenic strain were stained with PNab.
source: All NeonGreen-expressing nerve cells (684/684) were stained with PNab.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative counting data from the experiment.

claim: In the Hym176B line, 149/149 transgenic nerve cells were stained with PNab.
source: In the Hym176B line 149/149 transgenic nerve cells were stained with PNab.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative counting data from the experiment.

claim: In the nGreen line, 51/51 transgenic nerve cells were stained with PNab.
source: In the nGreen line 51/51 transgenic nerve cells were stained with PNab.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative counting data from the experiment.

claim: Both maceration and confocal imaging measurements yielded a ratio of 0.12 nerve cells per epithelial cell.
source: Both measurements yielded a ratio of 0.12 nerve cells/epithelial cell (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) confirming that PNab is a pan-neuronal marker staining all nerve cells in Hydra.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from both maceration and confocal imaging experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Nerve cell bodies in Hydra are roughly 10 µm long.
source: The nerve cell bodies are roughly 10 µm long; the distance between nerve cell bodies is variable in both ectoderm and endoderm but usually 50–100 µm.
evidence: The claim is based on measurements from confocal images.

claim: The distance between nerve cell bodies is variable in both ectoderm and endoderm but usually 50-100 µm.
source: The nerve cell bodies are roughly 10 µm long; the distance between nerve cell bodies is variable in both ectoderm and endoderm but usually 50–100 µm.
evidence: The claim is based on measurements from confocal images.

claim: No connections between nerve cells in the ectoderm and nerve cells in the endoderm were observed in complete rings of body column tissue from four different PNab-stained Lifeact polyps.
source: To search more extensively for nerve cell contacts between the ectoderm and endoderm, we imaged complete rings of body column tissue (see Figure 2B) from four different PNab-stained Lifeact polyps. These rings contained a total of 133 nerve cells (57 ectoderm, 76 endoderm) and associated neurites and represented about 4% of the body column tissue. No contacts between the ectodermal and endodermal nerve nets were observed.
evidence: The claim is supported by systematic imaging of tissue rings from multiple animals.

claim: There are no nerve cells in the endoderm of tentacles.
source: In his original description of the Hydra nerve net, Hadzi noted that nerve cells were not present in the endoderm of tentacles (Hadži, 1909). We have confirmed this unexpected result using PNab staining of Lifeact animals.
evidence: The claim is supported by PNab staining and confocal imaging data, and is consistent with historical observations by Hadži, 1909.

claim: The basal disk has very few nerve cells in the endoderm.
source: Similarly, the basal disk had very few nerve cells in the endoderm.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative cell counting data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The density of nerve cells in the body column endoderm is relatively constant (0.10-0.19) from the hypostome to the peduncle.
source: In contrast to these two differentiated structures, the density of nerve cells in the body column endoderm is relatively constant (0.10–0.19) from the hypostome to the peduncle.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative cell counting data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The ratio of nerve to epithelial cells in the ectoderm is relatively constant (0.15-0.22) in the gastric region and the peduncle.
source: The density of nerve cells in the ectoderm, however, changes dramatically along the body column. While the ratio of nerve to epithelial cells is relatively constant (0.15–0.22) in the gastric region and the peduncle, the number of nerve cells in the ectoderm rises sharply in the hypostome, tentacles, and basal disk.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative cell counting data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The number of nerve cells in the ectoderm rises sharply in the hypostome, tentacles, and basal disk.
source: While the ratio of nerve to epithelial cells is relatively constant (0.15–0.22) in the gastric region and the peduncle, the number of nerve cells in the ectoderm rises sharply in the hypostome, tentacles, and basal disk.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative cell counting data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Over long stretches the nerve net consists of bundles of neurites running parallel to each other.
source: This showed that over long stretches the nerve net consists of bundles of neurites running parallel to each other.
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging of GFP-labeled nerve cells overlapping with PNab-stained neurites shown in Figure 7.

claim: In the ectodermal nerve net, only about 20% of the cross-sectioned nerve tracks occurred as single neurites.
source: In the ectodermal nerve net, only about 20% of the cross-sectioned nerve tracks occurred as single neurites (Figure 9C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of TEM cross-sections shown in Figure 9C.

claim: About 80% of the nerve tracks in the ectoderm occurred as bundles, many as bundles of two neurites, but often also as bundles consisting of three to five neurites.
source: About 80% of the nerve tracks occurred as bundles, many as bundles of two neurites, but often also as bundles consisting of three to five neurites (Figure 9C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of TEM cross-sections shown in Figure 9C.

claim: About half of the endodermal nerve tracks were single neurites, the other half were bundles containing two neurites.
source: Second, about half of the endodermal nerve tracks were single neurites, the other half were bundles containing two neurites (Figure 9C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of TEM cross-sections shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Bundles with more than two neurites were not found in the endoderm.
source: Bundles with more than two neurites were not found in the endoderm.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of TEM cross-sections shown in Figure 9C.

claim: The ectodermal nerve net is more directly associated with muscle processes than the endodermal nerve net.
source: Thus, in summary, the ectodermal nerve net is more directly associated with muscle processes and clearly exhibits higher connectivity than the endodermal nerve net.
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM and confocal imaging data comparing ectoderm and endoderm.

claim: The ectodermal nerve net clearly exhibits higher connectivity than the endodermal nerve net.
source: Thus, in summary, the ectodermal nerve net is more directly associated with muscle processes and clearly exhibits higher connectivity than the endodermal nerve net.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of bundle complexity shown in Figure 9C.

claim: The distance between the two nerve cell bodies along the oral-aboral axis in the 3D reconstruction is roughly 50 μm.
source: The distance between the two nerve cell bodies along the oral-aboral axis is roughly 50 μm, in agreement with the distribution of nerve cell bodies shown in Figure 2C.
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements from the 3D reconstruction shown in Figure 10.

claim: There is only one ganglion nerve cell population in the endoderm (en1), and this population forms the endodermal nerve net.
source: Based on the Hydra single cell atlas, there is only one ganglion nerve cell population in the endoderm (en1), and this population forms the endodermal nerve net (Cazet et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to the Hydra single cell atlas (Cazet et al., 2023).

claim: En1 corresponds to the endodermal neural circuit RP2.
source: En1 corresponds to the endodermal neural circuit RP2 (Dupre and Yuste, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Dupre and Yuste, 2017.

claim: There are two nerve cell populations (ec1/ec5 and ec3) which form the nerve net in the ectoderm.
source: By comparison, there are two nerve cell populations (ec1/ec5 and ec3), which form the nerve net in the ectoderm.
evidence: The claim is based on the Hydra single cell atlas data.

claim: The ec1/ec5 and ec3 populations correspond to the contraction burst CB and RP1 neural circuits in the ectoderm.
source: These two populations correspond to the contraction burst CB and RP1 neural circuits in the ectoderm (Dupre and Yuste, 2017; Giez et al., 2023b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dupre and Yuste, 2017 and Giez et al., 2023b.

claim: Both ec1 and ec5 nerve cells, which form the CB neural circuit, express innexin 2.
source: Both ec1 and ec5 nerve cells, which form the CB neural circuit, express innexin 2; ec3 nerve cells, which form the RP1 neural circuit, express innexins 6 and 14 (Figure 12C).
evidence: The claim is supported by scRNAseq data shown in Figure 12C.

claim: Ec3 nerve cells, which form the RP1 neural circuit, express innexins 6 and 14.
source: Both ec1 and ec5 nerve cells, which form the CB neural circuit, express innexin 2; ec3 nerve cells, which form the RP1 neural circuit, express innexins 6 and 14 (Figure 12C).
evidence: The claim is supported by scRNAseq data shown in Figure 12C.

claim: Innexin 2 is also expressed in en1 nerve cells.
source: Innexin 2 is also expressed in en1 nerve cells (Figure 12C), which form the RP2 circuit in the endoderm.
evidence: The claim is supported by scRNAseq data shown in Figure 12C.

claim: There is no cross-correlation between the neural activity profiles of CB and RP2 and RP1 and RP2.
source: There is, however, no cross-correlation between the neural activity profiles of CB and RP2 and RP1 and RP2, indicating that the endodermal and ectodermal neural circuits are not connected (Dupre and Yuste, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to neural activity measurements by Dupre and Yuste, 2017.

claim: Most differentiating nerve cells without neurites on day 1 were not associated with the nerve net.
source: Migrating precursors without neurites do not associate with the nerve net and most differentiating nerve cells with short neurites on day 1 were also not associated with the nerve net (Figure 13D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from grafting experiments shown in Figure 13D.

claim: By days 2 and 3, most differentiating nerve cells extended neurites along the nerve net.
source: However, by days 2 and 3 most differentiating nerve cells extended neurites along the nerve net (Figure 13D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from grafting experiments shown in Figure 13D.

claim: Outgrowing neurites actively seek lateral associations with the neurites of the existing nerve net.
source: The results suggest that outgrowing neurites actively seek lateral associations with the neurites of the existing nerve net.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the time course data showing progressive association of differentiating nerve cells with the nerve net.

claim: Elimination of nerve cells leads to polyps that do not move and are incapable of capturing and ingesting prey.
source: This nerve net is required for control of spontaneous behavior: elimination of nerve cells leads to polyps that do not move and are incapable of capturing and ingesting prey (Campbell, 1976).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Campbell, 1976.

claim: The RP2 population is identical with the endodermal nerve net identified by PNab staining.
source: The RP2 population is identical with the endodermal nerve net identified by PNab staining (Figure 2D; Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of neural activity data with anatomical localization data.

claim: There are no RP2 nerve cells in the tentacles.
source: Moreover, there are no RP2 nerve cells in the tentacles, in agreement with the absence of endodermal nerve cells in the tentacles as assayed by PNab staining (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of neural activity data with PNab staining data.

claim: The activity of the CB network was directly correlated with rapid contraction of the body column.
source: The activity of the CB network was directly correlated with rapid contraction of the body column.
evidence: The claim is based on neural activity measurements by Dupre and Yuste, 2017.

claim: The activity of the RP1 and RP2 networks was associated with slower changes in behavior.
source: The activity of the RP1 and RP2 networks was associated with slower changes in behavior.
evidence: The claim is based on neural activity measurements by Dupre and Yuste, 2017.

claim: Both ectodermal and endodermal epithelial cells responded simultaneously to activity of the CB circuit during fast contraction of the body column.
source: This enabled detection of muscle activity in each epithelium during fast contraction of the body column initiated by CB nerve cells. The results showed that both ectodermal and endodermal epithelial cells responded simultaneously to activity of the CB circuit.
evidence: The claim is based on calcium imaging experiments by Szymanski and Yuste, 2019.

claim: Ectodermal epitheliomuscle cells activate endodermal epitheliomuscle cells directly via gap junction connections across the mesoglea.
source: Since there are no nerve cell connections between the ectoderm and the endoderm (see above), they postulated (Wang et al., 2023) that the ectodermal epitheliomuscle cells activate endodermal epitheliomuscle cells directly via gap junction connections across the mesoglea (Hand and Gobel, 1972).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that both epithelia respond simultaneously despite no neural connections, supported by citations to Wang et al., 2023 and Hand and Gobel, 1972.

claim: TEM studies have described both chemical synapses and gap junctions between nerve cells and ectodermal muscle processes.
source: Nerve cells in the ectoderm are closely associated with ectodermal muscle processes (Figures 4A, 9,, 10) and TEM studies have described both chemical synapses and gap junctions between nerve cells and ectodermal muscle processes (Westfall, 1973; Westfall et al., 1971; Westfall et al., 1980).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Westfall, 1973; Westfall et al., 1971; Westfall et al., 1980.

claim: There is no endodermal neural activity associated with the fast contraction of the body column.
source: By comparison, our results indicate that such contacts are rare in the endoderm (Figures 4B and 9D) and there is no endodermal neural activity associated with the fast contraction of the body column (Dupre and Yuste, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by neural activity measurements by Dupre and Yuste, 2017 and anatomical observations in the current study.

claim: Endodermal ganglion cells strongly express several neuropeptides, e.g., GLWa.
source: However, endodermal ganglion cells do strongly express several neuropeptides, e.g., GLWa (Cazet et al., 2023; Siebert et al., 2019) and release of such neuropeptides could modulate contractile activity in endodermal muscle processes.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cazet et al., 2023 and Siebert et al., 2019.

claim: GLWa induces slow contraction of the endoderm and consequently elongation of the body column.
source: In particular Takahashi et al., 2003, have shown that GLWa induces slow contraction of the endoderm and consequently elongation of the body column (Takahashi et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Takahashi et al., 2003.

claim: Ec1 and Ec1/5 express the neuropeptide Hym176.
source: Ec1 and Ec1/5 express the neuropeptide Hym176 (Noro et al., 2019) while Ec3 nerve cells express the neuropeptide GLWa.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Noro et al., 2019.

claim: Ec3 nerve cells express the neuropeptide GLWa.
source: Ec1 and Ec1/5 express the neuropeptide Hym176 (Noro et al., 2019) while Ec3 nerve cells express the neuropeptide GLWa.
evidence: The claim is based on scRNAseq data from Cazet et al., 2023 and Siebert et al., 2019.

claim: Nerve-free Hydra no longer contract and are nearly motionless due to the absence of ectodermal nerve cells.
source: This is clearly seen in nerve-free Hydra (Campbell, 1976; Marcum and Campbell, 1978). These animals no longer contract and are nearly motionless due to the absence of ectodermal nerve cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Campbell, 1976 and Marcum and Campbell, 1978.

claim: The body column of nerve-free animals is distended by increased osmotic pressure, which cannot be released through the closed mouth.
source: The body column of nerve-free animals is also distended by increased osmotic pressure, which cannot be released through the closed mouth.
evidence: The claim is based on observations of nerve-free animals.

claim: Regular experimental opening of the closed mouth in nerve-free animals leads to release of the gastric fluid and a return to normal tubular morphology of the body column.
source: However, regular experimental opening of the closed mouth in nerve-free animals leads to release of the gastric fluid and a return to normal tubular morphology of the body column (Wanek et al., 1980).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Wanek et al., 1980.

claim: One function of nerve cells in the endoderm is the control of endodermal muscle tension in response to osmotic pressure.
source: Thus, one function of nerve cells in the endoderm is the control of endodermal muscle tension in response to osmotic pressure.
evidence: The claim is inferred from observations of nerve-free animals and their response to mouth opening.

claim: Sensory cells constitute >50% of all endodermal nerve cells.
source: A striking feature of the endodermal nerve net is the large proportion of sensory cells, which constitute >50% of all endodermal nerve cells.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from confocal imaging.

claim: Endodermal sensory cells are oriented toward the gastric cavity and have sensory cilia which extend into the gastric cavity to monitor digestive activity and perhaps also osmotic strength.
source: These cells are oriented toward the gastric cavity (Figure 2B) and have sensory cilia, which extend into the gastric cavity to monitor digestive activity and perhaps also osmotic strength.
evidence: The claim is based on anatomical observations and inference about function.

claim: Endodermal ganglion cells (N4 nerve cells) are responsible for regulation of mouth opening and swelling of the body column.
source: Recent experiments of Giez et al., 2023a, have now shown that endodermal ganglion cells are responsible for this regulation. These N4 nerve cells fire in response to swelling of the body column, e.g., when a food pellet is present in the gut.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Giez et al., 2023a.

claim: Ablation of N4 nerve cells prevents mouth opening and ejection of the food pellet, which leads to dramatic bursting of the gut.
source: Ablation of N4 nerve cells using the nitroreductase-metronidazole system (Curado et al., 2007) prevents mouth opening and ejection of the food pellet, which leads to dramatic bursting of the gut.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to experimental results from Giez et al., 2023a.

claim: Expulsion of glass beads used as an artificial food pellet was significantly delayed in N4 ablated animals.
source: Expulsion of glass beads used as an artificial food pellet was also significantly delayed in N4 ablated animals.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to experimental results from Giez et al., 2023a.

claim: During digestion, slow waves of radial contraction move along the oral/aboral axis mixing the contents of the gut.
source: During digestion, slow waves of radial contraction move along the oral/aboral axis mixing the contents of the gut (Shimizu et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Shimizu et al., 2004.

claim: Both neck formation and radial contractions are absent or strongly reduced in nerve-free animals.
source: Both neck formation and radial contractions are absent or strongly reduced in nerve-free animals consistent with a role for the endodermal nerve net in regulating digestion.
evidence: The claim is based on observations of nerve-free animals.

claim: The complete absence of nerve cells in the endoderm of the tentacles is consistent with tentacles not being involved in digestion.
source: The complete absence of nerve cells in the endoderm of the tentacles (Figure 5), which are not involved in digestion, is consistent with this conclusion.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the anatomical observation and functional considerations.

claim: Nerve cell differentiation occurred throughout the body column and maintained the constant ratio of nerve cells to epithelial cells.
source: Nerve cell differentiation occurred throughout the body column and maintained the constant ratio of nerve cells to epithelial cells (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by tracking experiments cited in the text and data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The existing nerve net acts as a template for the addition of new nerve cells.
source: Both features are supported by our results and suggest that the existing nerve net acts as a template for the addition of new nerve cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the structural observations and growth dynamics.

claim: A fourth GCaMP6s activity pattern was identified in nerve cells at the base of tentacles, which was associated with movement of the head (nodding).
source: Indeed, a fourth GCaMP6s activity pattern was identified in nerve cells at the base of tentacles (Dupre and Yuste, 2017), which was associated with movement of the head (nodding).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Dupre and Yuste, 2017.

claim: A specific population of sensory nerve cells (Nv1) was identified which are incorporated into the battery cell complex in the ectoderm of tentacles.
source: A specific population of sensory nerve cells (Nv1) was identified which are incorporated into the battery cell complex in the ectoderm of tentacles (Hobmayer et al., 1990a; Hobmayer et al., 1990b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hobmayer et al., 1990a and Hobmayer et al., 1990b.

claim: A population of nerve cells in the lower peduncle express the innexin2 gene.
source: At the opposite end, in the lower peduncle, a population of nerve cells was identified, which express the innexin2 gene (Takaku et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Takaku et al., 2014.

claim: Elimination of the activity of innexin2 gap junctions disrupted contractile activity of the body column.
source: Elimination of the activity of these gap junctions disrupted contractile activity of the body column.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Takaku et al., 2014.

claim: Nerve cells in the endoderm are removed when endodermal tissue moves into tentacles.
source: As shown in Figures 5 and 6, there are no nerve cells in the endoderm of the tentacles, even though this tissue arises by displacement of body column tissue, which contains nerve cells in the endoderm. This implies that nerve cells in the endoderm are removed when endodermal tissue moves into tentacles.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that body column tissue contains endodermal nerve cells but tentacle tissue does not.

claim: Removal of endodermal nerve cells during tentacle formation likely occurs by apoptosis, although this has not been observed directly.
source: It appears likely that this occurs by apoptosis (Cikala et al., 1999), although this has not been observed directly.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference and citation to Cikala et al., 1999.

claim: PNab was made to a peptide in the classic cadherin of H. vulgaris.
source: Although PNab was made to a peptide in the classic cadherin of H. vulgaris, it is now clear that it does not recognize the cadherin protein.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the Materials and methods section.

claim: PNab does not recognize the cadherin protein.
source: Although PNab was made to a peptide in the classic cadherin of H. vulgaris, it is now clear that it does not recognize the cadherin protein.
evidence: The claim is based on sequence comparison showing the peptide sequence is not conserved in other Hydra species where PNab still stains neurons.

claim: Both H. oligactis and Hydra viridissima have classic cadherin proteins and nerve cells in both of these species stain strongly with PNab.
source: Both H. oligactis and Hydra viridissima have classic cadherin proteins and nerve cells in both of these species also stain strongly with PNab (Holstein, 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Holstein, 2023.

claim: The 18 amino acid sequence used to make the PNab antibody is only present in the H. vulgaris cadherin but not in the H. oligactis and H. viridissima cadherins.
source: In particular, the 18 amino acid sequence used to make the PNab antibody is only present in the H. vulgaris cadherin but not in the H. oligactis and H. viridissima cadherins.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 15.

claim: The identity of the PNab antigen is presently unknown.
source: Hence, it is clear that PNab cannot be staining cadherin in neurons and the identity of the PNab antigen is presently unknown.
evidence: The claim is stated directly based on the evidence that PNab cannot be recognizing cadherin.

claim: PNab is a highly specific reagent to identify nerve cells in all species of Hydra.
source: Nevertheless PNab is a highly specific reagent to identify nerve cells in all species of Hydra.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental validation across multiple Hydra species.

claim: Pre-absorption with the synthetic peptide blocked antibody staining.
source: Pre-absorption with the synthetic peptide blocked antibody staining (Cramer von Laue, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Cramer von Laue, 2003.

claim: Innexins have been shown to form gap junctions in Hydra.
source: Innexins have been shown to form gap junctions in Hydra (Alexopoulos et al., 2004; Takaku et al., 2014) and a search of an updated scRNAseq database for Hydra (Cazet et al., 2023) has revealed that the two nerve cell populations constituting the CB and RP1 circuits in the ectoderm (Dupre and Yuste, 2017), each contain distinct innexin transcripts.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Alexopoulos et al., 2004 and Takaku et al., 2014.

claim: Circuit-specific gap junctions can be formed by innexins uniquely expressed in nerve cells of each circuit.
source: Hence circuit-specific gap junctions can be formed by innexins uniquely expressed in nerve cells of each circuit.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that different neural circuits express different innexins.

claim: Nerve cells in Hydra arose early in the evolution of multicellular animals to sense the environment and control the activity of downstream effector cells.
source: Nerve cells arose early in the evolution of multicellular animals to sense the environment and control the activity of downstream effector cells (Anderson, 1990; Mackie, 1990).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Anderson, 1990 and Mackie, 1990.

claim: In non-bilaterians (cnidarians and ctenophores) nerve cells are organized in nerve nets.
source: In non-bilaterians (cnidarians and ctenophores) nerve cells are organized in nerve nets, which are often associated with muscle processes and coordinate the behaviors that involve ectodermal and endodermal tissues (Mackie, 1990).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Mackie, 1990.

claim: In bilaterian metazoans, nerves are organized into a centralized nervous system with large ganglia.
source: In bilaterian metazoans, the number of nerve cells is commonly much higher than in cnidarians and ctenophores and – importantly – nerves are organized into a centralized nervous system with large ganglia (Arendt et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Arendt et al., 2016.

claim: Hydra polyps live in fresh water and there is a constant influx of water into the cytoplasm of the epithelial cells.
source: Hydra polyps live in fresh water and there is a constant influx of water into the cytoplasm of the epithelial cells.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about Hydra physiology.

claim: Water is transferred to the gastric cavity and periodically voided through the mouth.
source: This water is transferred to the gastric cavity and periodically voided through the mouth (Benos and Prusch, 1972; Benos and Prusch, 1973; Yamamoto and Yuste, 2020) and potentially through the pore in the center of the basal disc (Shimizu et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Benos and Prusch, 1972; Benos and Prusch, 1973; Yamamoto and Yuste, 2020; and Shimizu et al., 2007.

claim: Following ingestion of prey, endodermal muscle processes below the tentacle ring contract locally ('neck formation') while endodermal muscles in the body column relax.
source: Two such events occur following ingestion of prey. First endodermal muscle processes below the tentacle ring contract locally ('neck formation') while endodermal muscles in the body column relax (Blanquet and Lenhoff, 1968).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Blanquet and Lenhoff, 1968.

claim: Neck formation and body column relaxation create a closed space in the gastric cavity for digestion of prey.
source: Together these events create a closed space in the gastric cavity for digestion of prey.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the description of neck formation and body column relaxation.

claim: After digestion is complete, slow contraction of endodermal muscle processes restores the normal columnar form of the body column.
source: After digestion is complete, slow contraction of endodermal muscle processes restores the normal columnar form of the body column.
evidence: The claim is based on observations of digestive behavior.
